intro: The Cajueiro de Pirangi looks like a small wood and is a single tree. A genetic quirk makes its branches grow sideways and root wherever they touch the ground, so one cashew planted in 1888 now covers roughly 8,500 square metres with a perimeter close to half a kilometre. Guinness World Records has listed it as the largest cashew tree in the world since 1994. It stands 12 kilometres south of Natal, behind its own gate, with walkways and a viewing tower for the crown.
meta_description: The Cajueiro de Pirangi is one cashew tree covering about 8,500 sqm, the world's largest since 1994. Walkways and a tower, 12km south of Natal.
question_meta: The Cajueiro de Pirangi, planted in 1888, is one cashew spread over about 8,500 square metres. Why it grows sideways, and how to reach it from Natal.
question_answer: The oldest tree in Pirangi is the Cajueiro de Pirangi, a cashew planted in 1888 and so about 138 years old. It is one specimen rather than a grove: its branches grow laterally and re-root where they meet the ground, which has spread a single tree across roughly 8,500 square metres. Guinness World Records recognised it in 1994 as the largest cashew tree in the world. Entry costs R$10, by card only, and the site opens daily from 8:00 to 17:30.
question_context: Almost every visitor arrives expecting an orchard and finds one trunk. The lateral growth is a mutation, not a planting scheme, and it compounds: each branch that touches soil roots and sends up new growth, which then does the same, so the area keeps changing and the published figures range from 7,300 to about 9,000 square metres depending on who measured and in which year. Botanists put the mass at roughly 70 ordinary cashew trees. The planting is credited to a fisherman, Luis Inacio de Oliveira, in 1888; local tradition adds that he died at 93 beneath it, a detail every source repeats and none of them documents. The Guinness record is not uncontested. A cashew in Piaui state was measured at about 8,800 square metres in a 2016 state tourism study, but no Guinness adjudicator has ever visited it, so Pirangi keeps the title. The current problem is the road: outer branches have reached the Rota do Sol highway running past the site, and holding the two apart is an ongoing maintenance job.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Pirangi?
faq.a: The Cajueiro de Pirangi, a cashew planted in 1888 and about 138 years old, recognised by Guinness World Records as the largest cashew tree in the world.

faq.q: Is it really one tree and not a grove?
faq.a: One tree. Its branches grow sideways instead of upward and root where they touch the ground, so what looks like a small wood of about 70 cashews is a single specimen covering roughly 8,500 square metres.
No. Entry costs R$10, payable by card only, and the site is open daily from 8:00 to 17:30, with shorter hours on 1 January and 25 December.
It sits 12 kilometres south of Natal at Pirangi do Norte. There is no rail; the drive along the Via Costeira and the RN-063 Rota do Sol takes about 20 to 25 minutes from the centre of Natal.

trees.story:
This looks like a small wood and it is one tree. A genetic quirk makes the branches of the Cajueiro de Pirangi grow sideways rather than upward, and where they touch the ground they root and carry on, so a single cashew has spread across something like 8,500 square metres. The published figures run from 7,300 to about 9,000, depending on who measured and in which year, because the tree keeps moving. Its perimeter is close to 500 metres. Botanists reckon the mass at around 70 ordinary cashew trees.

A fisherman called Luis Inacio de Oliveira planted it in 1888. Local tradition adds that he died at 93 beneath its branches, which is the sort of detail that survives because people enjoy repeating it rather than because anyone wrote it down. Guinness World Records listed it in 1994 as the largest cashew tree on earth and it has held the title since, though a rival in Piaui state claims a wider spread on the strength of a 2016 state tourism survey that no adjudicator ever came to check.

The tree's problem now is traffic. Its outer branches have reached the Rota do Sol highway beside the site, and keeping the two apart is a standing job for the people who look after it. Walkways run through the interior and a tower lets you see the whole crown, which from underneath is impossible.

best_time.label: November and December, when the cashew apples ripen

trees.access: Paid entry, R$10 (electronic payment only), open daily 8:00-17:30 (10:00-17:30 on Jan 1 and Dec 25, closed on election days). Walkways and a viewing tower let visitors see the whole crown.
trees.transport: 12 km south of Natal via Via Costeira then RN-063 (Rota do Sol); no rail, drive or taxi/bus, roughly 20-25 minutes from central Natal
